client: Lately, I’ve been feeling really overwhelmed at work, especially after my colleague pointed out my mistakes during last week’s team meeting. It’s been hard to focus, and I keep replaying that moment in my head, worrying that everyone thinks I’m not competent enough for this role. Honestly, I’m not sure if talking about it will help—I feel like I just need to figure it out on my own, but it’s really weighing on me.
therapist: It sounds like that moment in the meeting really stuck with you, and I hear how much it's affecting your confidence at work. While you say talking might not help, I notice your voice tightens when you describe replaying that moment—would you be willing to explore what makes that memory feel so particularly painful?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: It's painful because it wasn't just about the mistakes—it felt like my whole value as an employee was being questioned in front of everyone. I keep thinking that moment confirmed what I've secretly worried about all along... that I'm not as capable as I pretend to be. But I don't know if digging into this will help or just make me feel worse about myself.
therapist: I hear how deeply this connects to your fears about being "found out" as not good enough—that's such a vulnerable place to sit with. Your voice softens when you say "pretend," which makes me wonder if part of you might already be questioning whether that belief is entirely true?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I guess there is a part of me that knows I'm not completely faking it—I did get promoted last year after all. But then I think maybe that was just luck, or that they'll realize they made a mistake. It's exhausting constantly second-guessing myself like this.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two voices—one that recognizes your accomplishments and another that dismisses them as luck. I notice your speech quickens when you talk about second-guessing—does that pattern feel familiar from other areas of your life too?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Now that you mention it, I do this with friendships too—always wondering if people actually like me or just tolerate me. But work feels different somehow, more... measurable? Like my mistakes are right there in documents and emails for everyone to see. I don't know how to turn off this constant evaluation in my head.
therapist: It's interesting that you notice this pattern in friendships too—that constant evaluation seems to follow you, even though work feels more concrete with its paper trail. Your voice lifts slightly when you describe it as "measurable"—does that hint at why criticism at work might cut particularly deep for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: You're right—it does cut deeper because at work there's "proof" that I'm failing, while with friendships I can tell myself I'm just being paranoid. But now that we're talking about it, I'm realizing how exhausting it is to always be looking for proof of my worth. Still, I'm not sure what to do with this realization—knowing the pattern doesn't make it stop.
therapist: I hear both the exhaustion in your voice and that important insight about constantly seeking proof of your worth—that's a heavy burden to carry. The way your speech quickens makes me wonder if we might slow down together to explore what it would feel like to set that burden down, even just temporarily?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Setting it down sounds... terrifying, honestly. If I'm not constantly proving myself, how do I know I won't completely fall apart? But I'm also tired enough to admit I need to try something different. I just don't know where to start—it feels like my whole identity is tied up in being "the competent one."
therapist: It sounds like this idea of letting go feels both scary and necessary—your voice softens when you talk about being tired enough to try something different. Could we explore what "the competent one" protects you from, and what might happen if you allowed yourself to be something else, even just for a little while?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: "The competent one" protects me from feeling worthless, I guess. If I'm not good at my job, then who am I? Letting go of that feels like standing on the edge of a cliff—like I might just disappear if I'm not holding onto this identity. But I'm also realizing how much energy it takes to keep holding on, and I'm getting tired of it.
therapist: I hear both the fear of disappearing without this identity and the exhaustion of maintaining it—your voice gets very quiet when you describe that cliff edge. That image of holding on so tightly makes me wonder: who might you discover yourself to be if you loosened your grip, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: That's a really hard question to answer—I haven't let myself imagine who I could be outside of being "the competent one" in so long. Part of me wants to explore that, but another part feels like I'm betraying myself by even considering it. It's like I'm afraid that if I loosen my grip, I'll lose control completely and everything will fall apart.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between wanting to explore this new possibility and feeling like it would be a betrayal of who you've always been—that's such a vulnerable place to be. I notice your voice softens as you talk about losing control—could we explore what "everything falling apart" might actually look like, and whether there's a middle ground between holding on tight and letting go completely?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: When I think about "everything falling apart," I imagine losing my job, disappointing everyone around me, and ending up completely worthless. It's hard to imagine a middle ground because letting go at all feels like opening the floodgates—like I can't control how much I'll lose. But I also recognize that this might not be realistic, even if it feels true right now.
therapist: Your description of "opening the floodgates" paints such a vivid picture of how overwhelming this fear feels—like any movement toward change could lead to total loss. I notice that even as you recognize this might not be entirely realistic, your voice pitches higher when describing these fears—would you be willing to explore what a small, controlled "letting go" might look like, just as an experiment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I could maybe try something small, like admitting when I don't know something at work instead of pretending I have all the answers. But the idea still makes my stomach twist—what if people start seeing me as unreliable? I've built my whole career on being the person who always knows what to do.
therapist: It sounds like you're considering a brave step toward authenticity, even though it feels scary to risk that image of always knowing the answers. Your voice pitches higher when talking about being seen as unreliable—could we explore what it would mean if someone did see you that way, and whether that would necessarily change your overall value as an employee and person?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
